chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Alternatives Into Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Common Mistakes When Chasing Alternative Returns

children.text: Almost nobody loses money in alternatives because they lacked information. They lose money because a pitch arrived at the right moment, with the right story, and skipped past questions they already knew to ask. The 18% IRR sounded better than the Nifty. The "assured 12%" sounded like an FD. The friend's startup felt like a sure thing. This final lesson collects the most common mistakes Indian investors make when chasing alternative returns, groups them by where they happen, and gives you a last checklist to carry out of this course.

body.text: The costliest mistakes with alternatives are not exotic. They are ordinary errors of measurement, sizing, behaviour and verification, made under the pressure of a good story. Slow the decision down and most of them disappear.

children.text: Mistake Group 1: Measuring Returns Wrongly

cells: Comparing gross with net
A 14% gross P2P yield compared with the Nifty's net returns
Take off fees, costs, expected losses and tax first (Chapter 5)
Comparing unlike measures
A fund's IRR set against an index CAGR
Ask for the multiple and a PME check (Chapter 5)
Treating yield as return
A 10% InvIT yield assumed to be a 10% return
Check for return of capital and remaining asset life (Chapter 4)
Trusting smooth numbers
A fund that "never had a down year" treated as low risk
Unsmooth appraised returns and ask who values the holdings (Chapter 2)
Believing survivors
"Average IRR on exited deals: 17%"
Ask for returns across every deal, realised and unrealised (Chapter 1)

body.title: When the mistakes stack up
body.prompt: An investor in the 30% slab (31.2% with cess) picks a 14% gross yield lending product over a Nifty index fund. The product carries 2% in fees and 2% a year in expected credit losses, and its income is taxed yearly at slab rates. What is its expected post-tax return, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 14% − 2% fees − 2% expected losses = 10%. After tax: 10% × (1 − 0.312) ≈ 6.9%. The illustrative Nifty index fund in Chapter 5 delivered about 10.8% after costs and tax. A 2-point gross lead turned into a 4-point post-tax deficit, before counting the product's lock-in and default risk.

children.text: Mistake Group 2: Getting the Size Wrong
Locking up money with a job to do.
College fees, a down payment or retirement income placed in a 5 to 10-year lock-in.
Forgetting what you already own.
Adding a real estate fund to a portfolio already dominated by two flats, or pre-IPO shares on top of startup ESOPs.
Too few bets in a power-law asset.
Two or three angel investments, where the most likely result is losing money overall.
One giant ticket.
Stretching to meet a ₹1 crore AIF minimum that turns into 40% of investable wealth.
Leverage on top of illiquidity.
Borrowing to buy a second flat or unlisted shares, so a price fall and an EMI arrive together.
False diversification.
Six holdings in six wrappers that are all Indian equity and startup risk underneath.
Mistake Group 3: Behavioural Traps

body.title: What the trap says vs what to ask instead

columns.label: The trap
points: Recency: "It went up 60% in the last two years"
FOMO: "Only three slots left, closing Friday"
Authority: "Big family offices are all in this"
Exclusivity: "We only offer this to select clients"
Sunk cost: "I have already put in ₹40 lakh, so I should meet the next capital call and add more"
Overconfidence: "I know this sector, I work in it"

columns.label: The question to ask
points: What was the entry price, and what is the return from today's price?
If this is a good investment, why can it not wait a week?
Does their wealth, horizon and liquidity look anything like mine?
What is being hidden by keeping it exclusive?
Would I make this investment today if I owned none of it?
Is my job already a bet on this sector?

body.text: Alternatives magnify behavioural mistakes in two directions. Their lack of a daily price stops you panic-selling in a crash, which helps. But it also means you cannot correct a bad decision quickly, so an emotional purchase can stay locked in for a decade. The time to be disciplined is before you sign, not after.

children.text: Mistake Group 4: Skipping Verification

markDefs.definition: A pooled scheme in which investors' money is used to buy or develop assets, such as land or plantations, and returns are shared. In India, these must be registered with SEBI, and unregistered schemes are illegal.

children.text: The most expensive alternative mistakes in Indian history were not bad investments. They were not investments at all. PACL ran an unregistered
collective investment scheme

built on the promise of land and assured returns. SEBI's 2014 order found it had collected about ₹49,100 crore from crores of investors, and ordered it to refund them, a process that has taken many years. The Saradha collapse in West Bengal in 2013 followed a similar pattern of high promised returns and no real regulation. Both sold "alternative" assets with the language of safety.

body.caption: Who should be registered, and where to check

cells: An AIF, PMS or investment advice
SEBI
Exact entity name and registration number on SEBI's intermediary lists
Bonds or NCDs through an online platform
SEBI, as an online bond platform provider
The platform's registration and the issuer's credit rating
P2P lending
RBI, as an NBFC-P2P
RBI registration and the platform's disclosures on defaults
An REIT or SM REIT
SEBI
Registration, the offer document, and the listing status
Crypto trading
FIU-IND, for anti-money-laundering compliance
FIU-IND registration; remember it is not investor protection
An under-construction property
The state's RERA authority
Project registration, approvals and quarterly progress updates

body.label: SEBI: Recognised and Registered Intermediaries
body.description: Check whether an AIF, PMS provider, investment adviser, REIT or other intermediary is registered with SEBI before sharing any documents or money.

body.title: Red flags that should stop any alternative pitch
steps: "Assured" or "guaranteed" returns on anything linked to markets, property, startups or loans
Pressure to decide quickly, or limited slots closing within days
No SEBI, RBI or RERA registration you can verify yourself, or registration under a different entity name
No offer document, or refusal to give you time to read it
A buy-back promise with no clear legal structure or source of money
Returns quoted without fees, tax, time period or the full set of past deals
A single asset, tenant, borrower or project carrying the whole return
Payments requested to a personal account or an unrelated company

body.title: The sunk cost trap
body.question: Mehul has committed ₹1 crore to a VC fund. Four years in, it shows a paper loss and asks for the next ₹20 lakh capital call. A different manager offers him a "continuation" top-up to "average down." What is the soundest way to think about the extra top-up?
options: He must put in more to recover what he has lost
Evaluate the top-up as a brand-new investment: would he choose it today, at this size, given his current portfolio?
Always average down, since the J-curve means losses reverse
Refuse the committed capital call as well, since the fund is losing money
body.explanation: The committed capital call is a legal obligation he generally must meet. But any new, optional top-up should be judged fresh, as if he held nothing, using the sizing and scorecard tools. Past losses do not create a reason to add more, and the J-curve only reverses for funds that actually succeed.

body.title: Name the illusion
body.textWithBlank: Owning a PE fund, pre-IPO shares, angel investments and a mid-cap fund, all driven by Indian company valuations, gives only ___ diversification.
body.explanation: Different wrappers do not mean different risks. Real diversification comes from assets driven by different things, such as high-quality government bonds and gold alongside equity.

body.title: Capstone: the managed farmland pitch
body.scenario: Ankit and Deepa, both 38 and working in tech in Bengaluru, see an Instagram ad for "managed farmland" two hours from the city. For ₹25 lakh they get a fifth of an acre, managed by the company, with "assured 12% annual appreciation", organic produce delivered monthly, weekend cottage access, and a "buy-back option after 5 years." Their investable wealth is ₹90 lakh, their home is rented, and they want to buy a flat in 3 years.
body.prompt: Use tools from across the course to evaluate this pitch. Cover measurement, the four risks, sizing and verification.
body.modelAnswer:
Measurement:
- "Assured 12% appreciation" is not a return anyone can promise on land. There is no cash flow, so the price depends entirely on future buyers (Chapter 4).
- The produce and cottage access are consumption benefits, not investment returns, and the company's management fees reduce any gain.
- Real, post-tax return is unknown: stamp duty and registration, fees, and eventual capital gains tax all come off an estimated appreciation (Chapter 5).

The four risks (Chapter 2):
- Liquidity: very high. A fraction of a farm plot has few buyers. The buy-back is only as good as the company's finances and the legal terms.
- Valuation: very high. The company sets or influences the "value"; there is no market price.
- Leverage: low, unless they borrow to buy.
- Manager and governance: very high. Returns depend on one company's integrity and survival.

Legal and title: agricultural land purchase rules, land conversion, clear title and exactly what they legally own (a registered plot, a share in a company, or just a contract) must be checked by a property lawyer.

Sizing (Chapter 6):
- ₹25 lakh is about 28% of their ₹90 lakh, far above any sensible illiquid cap for their wealth (up to about 5%).
- Their flat purchase in 3 years means much of their wealth has a job, so lockable capital is low.

Verification red flags: assured returns, a social media ad, a buy-back promise without clear structure, and no SEBI-regulated structure or offer document.

Conclusion: this fails on almost every test. If they love the idea of farm weekends, that is a lifestyle purchase to fund from spare money, not an investment. Their priority should be protecting the flat down payment in liquid, lower-risk assets.

children.text: The Whole Course on One Page

body.caption: Six questions to ask about any alternative, one from each chapter
headers: What a good answer looks like

cells: 1. Two families of assets
Does it truly behave like an alternative, or just carry the label?
You can name its wrapper, pricing method and exit route
2. A wider lens on risk
What are its liquidity, valuation, leverage and manager risks, and how does it behave in a crash?
Risks you can see and size, not just a low volatility number
3. Traditional benchmarks
What would equity, fixed income or gold deliver over the same period?
A clear, fair benchmark with a similar horizon
4. Profiling the alternatives
Where does the return actually come from, and what is the typical outcome, not the best one?
Cash flows or a credible price driver, and realistic downside
5. Comparing like with like
What is the real, post-tax return, measured the right way?
A net figure that still beats the benchmark by enough to justify the extra risks
6. Putting it in your portfolio
Does it fit my gates, lockable capital, caps and existing holdings?
A size small enough that the worst case would not change your life

body.title: Course Recap: The Ideas to Remember

cards.definition: The wrapper, not the underlying asset, decides whether a holding behaves like a traditional or alternative asset.
Extra expected return for giving up the ability to sell, earned mainly through a lower entry price and only by those who hold to the end.
Infrequent, anchored valuations that make alternatives look less volatile and less correlated with equities than they really are.
In startup investing, a few big winners create most returns, so small portfolios usually miss them.
Lending's pattern of steady small gains and occasional large losses, clustered in stress years.
Running a fund's cash flows through an index to test whether it truly beat the public market.
Return after fees, costs, losses, tax and inflation, the only return that decides what you keep.
Investable wealth minus emergencies, goals within the lock-in and a buffer; a ceiling for illiquid alternatives, not a target.

points: Measurement mistakes, such as comparing gross with net or IRR with CAGR, can turn a 2-point gross lead into a 4-point post-tax deficit.
Sizing mistakes include locking up money with a job, ignoring existing property and ESOPs, too few power-law bets, and leverage on top of illiquidity.
Behavioural traps like recency, FOMO, exclusivity and sunk cost are strongest before you sign, and illiquidity makes them hard to undo.
The most damaging schemes in Indian history, such as PACL and Saradha, were unregistered and promised assured returns, so always verify registration yourself.
Any assured return, pressure to decide fast, unverifiable registration or unclear buy-back should stop a pitch immediately.
Before any alternative, ask the six chapter questions: behaviour, risks, benchmark, return source, real return and fit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Examples, investors and figures are illustrative, and references to past regulatory actions are summaries of public events. Verify registrations directly with SEBI, RBI or the relevant RERA authority, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser, a qualified tax professional and, for property, a lawyer before making decisions.
